title: The Stack push and pop
summary: The stack is memory that grows downwards from a high address, and rsp always points at its top. push moves rsp down 8 bytes and stores a value; pop loads it and moves rsp back up. It saves registers that must be kept, holds temporary space reserved with sub rsp, and must end exactly where it started.
markdown:
## A stack of plates

The **stack** is a region of memory the operating system gives every program, a few megabytes in size. `rsp` points at the item on top. It **grows downwards**: pushing makes `rsp` smaller.

| Instruction | Same as |
|---|---|
| `push rax` | `sub rsp, 8` then `mov [rsp], rax` |
| `pop rbx` | `mov rbx, [rsp]` then `add rsp, 8` |

The last thing pushed is the first popped: a "last in, first out" stack.

```demo-asm
title: push and pop
init: rax=11, rbx=22, rcx=33
    push rax
    push rbx
    push rcx
    pop rax
    pop rbx
    pop rcx
    ret
```

Step through and watch `rsp` and the values on the stack. Popping in the same order as pushing **reverses** them: afterwards rax = 33 and rcx = 11.

## Saving registers

The most common use: keeping a register's value safe while you need the register for something else. A function that wants to use `rbx` (which it must give back unchanged) saves it first:

```nasm-norun
sum_squares:            ; rdi = a, rsi = b; returns a*a + b*b
        push    rbx             ; save the caller's rbx
        mov     rbx, rdi
        imul    rbx, rdi        ; rbx = a * a
        mov     rax, rsi
        imul    rax, rsi        ; rax = b * b
        add     rax, rbx
        pop     rbx             ; give rbx back
        ret
```

Pops must match pushes, in **reverse order**: `push rbx`, `push r12` ... `pop r12`, `pop rbx`.

## Temporary space

Subtracting from `rsp` reserves bytes on the stack; adding gives them back. This is how functions get local arrays and buffers without `.bss`:

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .text
_start:
        sub     rsp, 16                 ; 16 bytes of space at [rsp] to [rsp + 15]
        mov     byte [rsp], 'O'
        mov     byte [rsp + 1], 'K'
        mov     byte [rsp + 2], '!'
        mov     byte [rsp + 3], 10
        mov     eax, 1
        mov     edi, 1
        mov     rsi, rsp                ; the address of the bytes on the stack
        mov     edx, 4
        syscall
        add     rsp, 16                 ; give the space back
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

## Reversing with the stack

Since the stack reverses order, it can turn a string around: push every character, then pop them back in:

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .data
text:   db      "stressed", 0

        section .text
_start:
        lea     rsi, [rel text]
        xor     ecx, ecx                ; how many pushed
.push:  movzx   eax, byte [rsi + rcx]
        test    al, al
        jz      .popping
        push    rax
        inc     rcx
        jmp     .push
.popping:
        xor     edx, edx
.pop:   cmp     rdx, rcx
        jae     .done
        pop     rax
        mov     [rsi + rdx], al
        inc     rdx
        jmp     .pop
.done:
        lea     rdi, [rel text]
        call    print_str               ; desserts
        call    print_newline
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

## Rules

> [!warning] Leave the stack as you found it
> - Every `push` needs a `pop` (or an `add rsp`) before the function returns, or `ret` will jump to a wrong address (lesson 5.01 shows why) and the program crashes.
> - Never read below `rsp` after the space is given back: the next push or system call overwrites it.
> - Before calling a function, `rsp` must be a multiple of **16** (lesson 5.02). The routines in this course do not mind, but C functions can crash otherwise.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What does push rax do?
- Stores rax at [rsp] and moves rsp up
- Copies rax into rsp
+ Moves rsp down by 8 and stores rax at the new [rsp]
> The stack grows downwards.

? After push rax, push rbx, pop rax, pop rbx - what happened?
- Nothing changed
+ rax and rbx were swapped
- Both hold the old rbx
> Last in, first out.

? How does a function make room for 32 bytes of local space?
- With push 32
+ With sub rsp, 32, undone before ret
- With mov rsp, 32
> Subtracting from rsp reserves space on the stack; add rsp, 32 gives it back before returning.

? A function pushes rbx and r12 at the start. In which order should it pop them?
- pop rbx, then pop r12
+ pop r12, then pop rbx
- Either
> Reverse order.
```
